title: Where it grows
subtitle: Bordeaux and beyond
objectives: Explain why it suits clay and cool soils

steps.title: A wide map
steps.body: Merlot is the most planted grape in Bordeaux, about 60% of red plantings. It's important in Italy, especially Tuscany and Friuli, and in Switzerland's Ticino. In the New World it grows in California, Washington, Chile, Australia, South Africa and New Zealand's Hawke's Bay.

steps.title: Early and clay-loving
steps.body: Merlot buds and ripens one to two weeks before Cabernet Sauvignon. On cool, water-retentive clay soils, where Cabernet would struggle to ripen, Merlot thrives. But early budding exposes it to spring frost, and its thinner skins make it prone to rot in wet weather, and to coulure, poor fruit set.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Merlot role.
steps.explanation: Merlot is grown widely, often in Bordeaux-style blends.

steps.body: When a Bordeaux label says Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur, without a famous commune, it's often Merlot-dominated and made to drink early.

steps.prompt: What are Merlot's vulnerabilities in the vineyard?
steps.explanation: Merlot ripens easily; in heat it can overripen, not fail to ripen.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape, grown worldwide
It ripens early and loves cool clay soils
Frost, rot and coulure are its weaknesses
